Hilbert Space

In short, Hilbert Space is a complete inner-product space that is infinite-dimesional.

Definition 1 (Hilbert Space)

Let XXX be a complex vector space. An inner product is a function from X×X→CX \times X \to \mathbb{C}X×X→C

(x,y)↦⟨x,y⟩(x,y)\mapsto \langle x,y \rangle(x,y)↦⟨x,y⟩
(1)

if it satisfies, ∀x,y,z∈X\forall x,y, z \in X∀x,y,z∈X

  1. ⟨ax+by,z⟩=a⟨x,z⟩+b⟨y,z⟩\langle ax+by, z\rangle=a\langle x,z \rangle + b\langle y, z\rangle⟨ax+by,z⟩=a⟨x,z⟩+b⟨y,z⟩

  2. ⟨x,y⟩=⟨y,x⟩‾\langle x,y \rangle = \overline{\langle y, x\rangle}⟨x,y⟩=⟨y,x⟩​

  3. (x,z)∈(0,∞)(x,z)\in (0,\infty)(x,z)∈(0,∞)

The pair (X,⟨⋅,⋅⟩)(X,\langle \cdot, \cdot\rangle)(X,⟨⋅,⋅⟩) is a pre-Hilbert space. It is also a Banach Space with norm induced by the inner product:

∥⋅∥=⟨⋅,⋅⟩1/q\|\cdot \| = \langle\cdot, \cdot \rangle^{1/q}∥⋅∥=⟨⋅,⋅⟩1/q
(2)

If XXX is also complete, it is a Hilbert Space

The Riez Representation Theorem¶

Theorem 1 (Riez Representation Theorem)

Let f∈H∗f\in H^*f∈H∗, ∃!\exists !∃! y∈Hy\in Hy∈H such that ∀x∈H\forall x\in H∀x∈H we have:

f(x)=⟨x,y⟩f(x)=\langle x,y \ranglef(x)=⟨x,y⟩
(3)

The Basis Theorem¶

Theorem 2 (Bessel’s Inequality)

If {uα}α∈A\{u_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha \in A}{uα​}α∈A​ is an orthonormal set in HHH, then for any x∈Hx\in Hx∈H:

∑α∈A∣⟨x,uα⟩∣2≤∥x∥2\sum_{\alpha \in A}|\langle x, u_{\alpha}\rangle|^2 \leq \|x\|^2α∈A∑​∣⟨x,uα​⟩∣2≤∥x∥2

Note this implies {α:⟨x,uα⟩≠0}\{\alpha: \langle x,u_{\alpha} \rangle\neq 0\}{α:⟨x,uα​⟩=0} is countable

Theorem 3 (Basis Theorem)

If {uα}α∈A\{u_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha \in A}{uα​}α∈A​ is an orthonormal set then the following are equivalent:

  1. (Completeness) If ⟨x,uα⟩=0,∀α∈A\langle x,u_{\alpha}\rangle =0, \forall \alpha \in A⟨x,uα​⟩=0,∀α∈A then x=0x=0x=0

  2. (Parseval’s Identity) ∀x∈H\forall x\in H∀x∈H

    ∥x∥2=∑α∈A∣⟨x,uα⟩∣2\|x\|^2 = \sum_{\alpha \in A} |\langle x, u_{\alpha} \rangle|^2∥x∥2=α∈A∑​∣⟨x,uα​⟩∣2
    (5)

  3. (Representation) ∀x∈H\forall x\in H∀x∈H

    x=∑α∈A⟨x,uα⟩uαx = \sum_{\alpha \in A} \langle x, u_{\alpha} \rangle u_{\alpha}x=α∈A∑​⟨x,uα​⟩uα​
    (6)

∑j=1∞⟨x,uαj⟩uαj=∑α∈A⟨x,uα⟩uα\sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \langle x, u_{\alpha_j}\rangle u_{\alpha_j}=\sum_{\alpha \in A} \langle x, u_{\alpha}\rangle u_{\alpha}j=1∑∞​⟨x,uαj​​⟩uαj​​=α∈A∑​⟨x,uα​⟩uα​

Using orthonormality we have[1]:

∥∑nm⟨x,uαj⟩uαj∥2=⟨∑nm⟨x,uαj⟩uαj,∑nm⟨x,uαk⟩uαk⟩=∑nm∣⟨x,uαk⟩∣2\begin{align*} \left \| \sum_{n}^m \langle x, u_{\alpha_j} \rangle u_{\alpha_j} \right \|^2 &= \left\langle \sum_{n}^m \langle x, u_{\alpha_j} \rangle u_{\alpha_j}, \sum_{n}^m \langle x, u_{\alpha_k} \rangle u_{\alpha_k} \right\rangle \\ &= \sum_{n}^m \left| \langle x, u_{\alpha_k} \rangle \right|^2 \end{align*}∥∥​n∑m​⟨x,uαj​​⟩uαj​​∥∥​2​=⟨n∑m​⟨x,uαj​​⟩uαj​​,n∑m​⟨x,uαk​​⟩uαk​​⟩=n∑m​∣⟨x,uαk​​⟩∣2​

The Sturm-Liouville Operator¶

The Sturm-Liouville operator is a linear differential operator of the form

L=−ddx(pddxy)+qddx\mathcal L=-\frac{d}{dx}\left(p\frac{d}{dx}y\right)+q\frac{d}{dx}L=−dxd​(pdxd​y)+qdxd​
(10)

We’ve shown that the Sturm-Liouville opeartor is self-adjoint with appropriate boundary condition in the sense that:

⟨u,Lv⟩=⟨L∗u,v⟩\begin{align*} \langle u, \mathcal Lv \rangle &= \langle \mathcal L^*u, v \rangle \end{align*}⟨u,Lv⟩​=⟨L∗u,v⟩​
(11)

hence it is analgous to self-adjoint operator in finite-dimensional vector spaces, which as symmetric matrix representation when the underlying field is real. We now make this connection explicit, i.e., actually constructing the discretized, finite-dimensional matrix representation of the Sturm-Liouville Operator.

A Discrete Analog¶

Let’s consider a concrete SL opeartor defined on [0,1][0,1][0,1] with Dirchlet boundary condition y(0)=y(1)=0y(0)=y(1)=0y(0)=y(1)=0. Instead of directly discretizing L\mathcal LL, we aim to find a matrix LLL such that discretizes the quadratic form:

F(y)=∫yLydx→y^TLy^F(y)=\int y\mathcal Ly dx \rightarrow \hat y^TL\hat yF(y)=∫yLydx→y^​TLy^​
(12)

First we note that:

F(y)=∫01y(−ddx(pddxy)+qy)dx=∫01−yddx(pddxy)dx+∫01qy2dx=−{[ypdydx]01−∫p(dydx)2}+∫01qy2dx=∫01py′2+qy2\begin{align*} F(y) &= \int_0^1 y\left(-\frac{d}{dx}\left(p\frac{d}{dx}y\right) + qy\right) dx \\ &= \int_0^1 -y \frac{d}{dx}\left(p\frac{d}{dx}y\right)dx+\int_0^1 qy^2dx \\ &= -\left\{\cancel{\left[yp\frac{dy}{dx}\right]_0^1} - \int p\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2 \right\} + \int_0^1 qy^2dx \\ &= \int_0^1 py'^2 + qy^2 \end{align*}F(y)​=∫01​y(−dxd​(pdxd​y)+qy)dx=∫01​−ydxd​(pdxd​y)dx+∫01​qy2dx=−{[ypdxdy​]01​​−∫p(dxdy​)2}+∫01​qy2dx=∫01​py′2+qy2​
(13)

Now we discretize y,p,qy, p, qy,p,q to NNN-dimensional arrays:

y^=[y1,...,yN]p^=[p1,...,pN]q^=[q1,...,qN]\begin{align*} \hat y &= [y_1,...,y_N] \\ \hat p &= [p_1,...,p_N] \\ \hat q &= [q_1,...,q_N] \end{align*}y^​p^​q^​​=[y1​,...,yN​]=[p1​,...,pN​]=[q1​,...,qN​]​
(14)

Using forward difference we get:

y^=(yi+1−yih)2\hat y =\left(\frac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{h}\right)^2y^​=(hyi+1​−yi​​)2
(15)

Rewrite the integral as a finite sum we obtain a discretized version of (13):

F^(y^)=∑i=1Nhpi(yi+1−yih)2+qiyi2\boxed{\hat F(\hat y)=\sum_{i=1}^N h p_i\left(\frac{y_{i+1}-y_i}{h}\right)^2 +q_iy_i^2}F^(y^​)=i=1∑N​hpi​(hyi+1​−yi​​)2+qi​yi2​​
(16)

Our goal is now to find a matrix L LL such that y^TLy^=F^(y^)\hat y^TL\hat y=\hat F(\hat y)y^​TLy^​=F^(y^​). Rewrite F^(y^)\hat F(\hat y)F^(y^​):

F^(y^)=∑i=1NNpi(yi+12−2yi+1yi+yi2)+1Nqiyi2\hat F(\hat y) =\sum_{i=1}^N Np_i(y_{i+1}^2 -2y_{i+1}y_i +y_i^2)+\frac{1}{N}q_iy_i^2F^(y^​)=i=1∑N​Npi​(yi+12​−2yi+1​yi​+yi2​)+N1​qi​yi2​
(17)

We can split L=L1+L2L=L_1+L_2L=L1​+L2​ such that

  1. y^TL1y^=∑i=1NNpi(yi+12−2yi+1yi+yi2)\hat y^T L_1 \hat y = \sum_{i=1}^N Np_i(y_{i+1}^2 -2y_{i+1}y_i +y_i^2)y^​TL1​y^​=∑i=1N​Npi​(yi+12​−2yi+1​yi​+yi2​)

  2. y^TL2y^=∑i=1N1Nqiyi2\hat y^T L_2 \hat y = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{N}q_iy_i^2y^​TL2​y^​=∑i=1N​N1​qi​yi2​.

(Constructing L1L_1L1​) Let’s first deal with L1L_1L1​. Consider the 2×22\times 22×2block with the upperleft corner at (i,i)(i,i)(i,i) that should represent Npi(yi+12−2yi+1yi+yi2)Np_i(y_{i+1}^2 -2y_{i+1}y_i +y_i^2)Npi​(yi+12​−2yi+1​yi​+yi2​). This is easy:

Ai=Npi(1−1−11)A_i=Np_i\begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1\\ -1 & 1 \\ \end{pmatrix}Ai​=Npi​(1−1​−11​)
(18)

To assemble L1L_1L1​ we can overlap AiA_iAi​ along the diagonal of LLL with a stride of 1. Concretely:

for i=1,...,N-1
    L[i,i] += Np_i
    L[i+1,i+1] += Np_i
    L[i,i+1] -= Np_i 
    L[i+1,i] -= Np_i
Example 1

A quick example for N=4N=4N=4:

4(p1−p100−p1p1+p2−p200−p2p2+p3−p300−p3p3)4\begin{pmatrix} p_1 & -p_1 & 0 & 0 \\ -p_1 & p_1+p_2 & -p_2 &0 \\ 0 & -p_2 & p_2+p_3 & -p_3 \\ 0 & 0 & -p_3 & p_3 \end{pmatrix}4⎝⎛​p1​−p1​00​−p1​p1​+p2​−p2​0​0−p2​p2​+p3​−p3​​00−p3​p3​​⎠⎞​
(19)

(Constructing L2L_2L2​) L2L_2L2​ is purely diagonal and is easier to derive. Since it only has quadratic term yi2y_i^2yi2​, at each row iii we only need to include yiy_iyi​. Hence:

L2=1N(q1⋱qN)L_2 = \frac{1}{N}\begin{pmatrix}q_1 & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & q_N \end{pmatrix}L2​=N1​⎝⎛​q1​​⋱​qN​​⎠⎞​
(20)

(Assembly L1+L2L_1+L_2L1​+L2​) It is clear that LLL should look like:

L=N(p1−p1−p1p1+p2−p2⋱⋱⋱−pN−1pN−1+pN−pN−pNpN)+1N(q1⋱qN)L=N\begin{pmatrix} p_1& -p_1 & & & \\ -p_1& p_1+p_2 & -p_2 & & \\ & \ddots & \ddots & \ddots & \\ & &-p_{N-1} &p_{N-1}+p_{N} & -p_N \\ & & &-p_N & p_N \\ \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{N}\begin{pmatrix}q_1 & & \\ & \ddots & \\ & & q_N \end{pmatrix}L=N⎝⎛​p1​−p1​​−p1​p1​+p2​⋱​−p2​⋱−pN−1​​⋱pN−1​+pN​−pN​​−pN​pN​​⎠⎞​+N1​⎝⎛​q1​​⋱​qN​​⎠⎞​
(21)

However, since we are dealing with concrete operators with accompanying domain and boundary condition, we need to encoorperate the Dirchelt boundary condition y(0)=1,y(1)=0y(0)=1, y(1)=0y(0)=1,y(1)=0 into LLL. To do so we need to zero-out the first row and column of LLL. Hence finally we get:

Proposition 1

The Sturm-Liouville Operator on [0,1][0,1][0,1] with Dirchlet boundary condition y(0)=y(1)y(0)=y(1)y(0)=y(1) can be discretized as

L=N(000p1+p2−p2−p2⋱⋱−pN−1⋱−pN−1pN−1+pN000)+1N(0q2⋱qN−10)L=N\begin{pmatrix} 0 &0 & & & &\\ 0 &p_1+p_2 & -p_2& & & \\ &-p_2& \ddots &\ddots & -p_{N-1}& \\ & & \ddots &-p_{N-1} & p_{N-1}+p_N &0 \\ & & & &0 & 0\\ \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{N}\begin{pmatrix}0 & & & & \\ & q_2 & & & \\ & & \ddots& & \\ & & & q_{N-1} & \\ & & & & 0 \\ \end{pmatrix}L=N⎝⎛​00​0p1​+p2​−p2​​−p2​⋱⋱​⋱−pN−1​​−pN−1​pN−1​+pN​0​00​⎠⎞​+N1​⎝⎛​0​q2​​⋱​qN−1​​0​⎠⎞​
(22)

We can see that LLL is indeed a symmetric real matrix(Hermitian)!

Numpy Implementation This can easily be translated to naive numpy code:

class SturmLiouville:
    def __init__(self,N, p, q=None, grid='forward'):
        A = np.zeros(shape=(N,N))
        if grid == 'forward':
            for i in range(N-1):
                A[i, i] += p[i]
                A[i+1, i+1] += p[i]
                A[i, i+1] -= p[i]
                A[i+1, i] -= p[i]

        if q is not None:
            I = np.eye(N) 
            L = A + q @ I
        else:
            L = A
        
        # Dirchlet Boundary Condition
            L[0,0]=0.0
            L[0,1]=0.0
            L[1,0]=0.0
            L[N-1,N-1]=0.0
            L[N-1,N-2]=0.0
            L[N-2,N-1]=0.0
        self.L = (L * N ** 2)
        self.N = N

    def solve_eigen(self, top_k=10):
        eval, evec = np.linalg.eig(self.L)
        top_k_idx = np.argsort(eval[eval>0])[:top_k]
        return eval[top_k_idx] , evec[:, top_k_idx], top_k_idx
